Hi Alex / Priya — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can align with your engineering team: 

1) Goals we heard:
- Primary integration is an in-product assistant (chat) for support workflows; later expansion to automated summarization and search re-ranks.
- Need predictable latency (P95 < 300ms) for short prompt flows and support bulk embedding jobs for nightly re-ranks.
- Security: data stays in your VPC, keys managed by your KMS.

2) Immediate asks from your side (from call):
- SDK setup & auth model options
- Routing: multi-model / fallback behavior when Dedicated capacity is constrained
- Structured output / tool calling & how Redwood supports validators
- Question about request/response schema differences: chat vs completions, tokenization, max_tokens/stop behavior, streaming semantics

I've looped in Rafael (solutions) and Vivek (architecture) to give a concise technical answer below.

From: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acme.com>, Priya Desai <priya.desai@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Acme - follow-up: SDK, auth, routing + RSP schema Qs (technical note)

Hi Alex / Priya — Rafael from Solutions Engineering here. Below is a consolidated, pragmatic answer to the items you called out. I included short examples you can try in the SDK. If you want a sandbox we can provision a test key scoped to your Dedicated pool.

1) SDK setup & auth - Options: API key (standard), mTLS (if using Private VPC), and short-lived tokens via our control-plane for constrained clients.
- API key: easiest for PoC. Keys can be scoped by model/route and rotated via the Console.
- mTLS: recommended for on-prem or for customers requiring cert-based mutual auth. Redwood Private supports client cert authentication to the local gateway.
- KMS/HSM: we integrate with major KMS providers; your encryption-at-rest and envelope keys can be customer-managed.

2) Routing / multi-model fallback - You can declare routing policies in the request header or in a config file: priority -> preferred model variants -> fallback tier. Example policy semantics: first try "redwood-chat-8k-quant" (low cost), fallback to "redwood-chat-8k-fp16" for quality, final fallback to hosted generic endpoint. The runtime adds automatic model variant compatibility checks; if a model doesn't support streaming/ tools, the router will pick a variant that does.

3) Structured output / tool-calling - We support function/tool calling in the chat endpoint. For strict JSON outputs we recommend:
- Use a JSON schema in the system message (or pass it in as a validation schema on the request).
- Enable strict-mode output validation server-side so partial outputs result in a structured error and an alternative non-strict response.
- For streaming + strict JSON: stream token deltas but accumulate on the server and run an incremental parser with best-effort repairs. In practice we surface two patterns: 
  a) server-validated: request completes, we return validated JSON (recommended for critical flows),
  b) streaming-first: you get partial deltas for UI, then a final validated payload in the completion webhook or final frame.

Examples (pseudo-shell):
- Chat (preferred for tool-calling / structured output):
POST /v1/chat/completions
Authorization: Bearer $KEY

{
  "model": "redwood-chat-8k",
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are an assistant that outputs JSON matching schema X."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Get me the top 3 related articles for 'billing errors'."}
  ],
  "functions": [ {"name":"search_articles","parameters":{...}} ],
  "return_tool_calls": true
}

- Completions (older flow; simpler text-only responses):
POST /v1/completions
{
  "model": "redwood-complete-2",
  "prompt": "System: You are...
User: Find top 3 articles for billing errors:
",
  "max_tokens": 400,
  "stop": ["

"]
}

4) Chat vs Completions (key differences) - Chat endpoints expect structured message arrays (role/content) and have first-class support for function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs. Completions are token-prompt-based and better for older code paths or simple single-turn text outputs.
- Token accounting: Chat messages are converted into a serialized token stream before inference; tokenization is the same under the hood (model-specific). However, some SDK helpers will precompute token counts for you.

5) Tokenization and max_tokens semantics - max_tokens: limits the number of tokens generated in the response, not counting the prompt tokens. For chat: prompt includes all message history. For completions: prompt is the single prompt string.
- If prompt + max_tokens exceeds model context window, the request will be rejected or older messages will be truncated depending on your session policy. We expose truncation strategies (head/trailing/system-preserve).
- Stop sequences: in completions you can pass stop strings; the server will stop emitting further tokens when a stop sequence is sampled. For chat, stop is supported but we also recommend schema-based termination for JSON.

6) Streaming semantics & partial JSON - When streaming is enabled you receive token deltas as they are produced. Important notes: 
  - Partial streams can contain incomplete JSON (e.g., you may receive "{ \"name\": \"Billing""), so client-side incremental parsers must handle partial tokens and reassembly.
  - For strict JSON needs: use server-side validation or post-stream reparse and repair.
  - If you rely on streaming to extract quick values (like an ID), consider emitting a small stable prefix followed by the JSON payload (e.g., "ID: 12345
{...}") so the prefix is safe to parse mid-stream.

7) Embeddings & rerankers - Embedding calls are simple: POST /v1/embeddings with a batch of texts. For reranking we recommend a 2-step flow: generate embeddings + run approximate nearest-neighbor search (we can host FAISS clusters) + rerank top-K with a lightweight cross-encoder call if you need semantic rescoring.

8) Practical gotchas - Beware of:
  - stop sequences that are substrings of the schema tokens (use explicit termination tokens or schema validation)
  - using streaming alone for critical structured outputs (combine with server-side final validation)
  - prompt + assistant history growth exceeding context; set a truncation policy early in integration

If helpful, I can produce a short test harness (node/python) that:
- sends a chat request with function definitions and simulates streaming,
- records the token counts & shows how stop sequences interact with partial JSON,
- runs the embedding -> ANN -> rerank flow on a small dataset.

Let me know which test you'd like first and we can spin up a sandbox key.

Cheers,
Rafael Mendes
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
